claim: Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic structural component of excitatory synapses.
source: Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic structural component of excitatory synapses, and their experience-dependent plasticity has been extensively studied in mouse superficial cortex using two-photon microscopy in vivo.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the structural role of dendritic spines in synaptic architecture.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity of dendritic spines has been extensively studied in mouse superficial cortex using two-photon microscopy in vivo.
source: Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic structural component of excitatory synapses, and their experience-dependent plasticity has been extensively studied in mouse superficial cortex using two-photon microscopy in vivo.
evidence: This statement references the existing body of literature on spine plasticity studies in cortex.

claim: Very little is known about spine plasticity in the hippocampus.
source: By contrast, very little is known about spine plasticity in the hippocampus, which is the archetypical memory center of the brain, mostly because it is difficult to visualize dendritic spines in this deeply embedded structure with sufficient spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on the state of the literature.

claim: The hippocampus is the archetypical memory center of the brain.
source: By contrast, very little is known about spine plasticity in the hippocampus, which is the archetypical memory center of the brain, mostly because it is difficult to visualize dendritic spines in this deeply embedded structure with sufficient spatial resolution.
evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about the hippocampus's role in memory.

claim: It is difficult to visualize dendritic spines in the hippocampus with sufficient spatial resolution because it is a deeply embedded structure.
source: By contrast, very little is known about spine plasticity in the hippocampus, which is the archetypical memory center of the brain, mostly because it is difficult to visualize dendritic spines in this deeply embedded structure with sufficient spatial resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of the hippocampus and technical limitations of imaging.

claim: The authors developed chronic 2P-STED microscopy in mouse hippocampus using a 'hippocampal window' based on resection of cortical tissue and a long working distance objective.
source: We developed chronic 2P-STED microscopy in mouse hippocampus, using a 'hippocampal window' based on resection of cortical tissue and a long working distance objective for optical access.
evidence: This is a methodological development described in the manuscript with supporting experimental details.

claim: The authors observed a two-fold higher spine density than previous studies.
source: We observed a two-fold higher spine density than previous studies and measured a spine turnover of ~40% within 4 days, which depended on spine size.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' measurements compared to literature values.

claim: The authors measured a spine turnover of ~40% within 4 days.
source: We observed a two-fold higher spine density than previous studies and measured a spine turnover of ~40% within 4 days, which depended on spine size.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the longitudinal imaging experiments.

claim: Spine turnover depends on spine size.
source: We observed a two-fold higher spine density than previous studies and measured a spine turnover of ~40% within 4 days, which depended on spine size.
evidence: This is a finding from the morphological analysis of spine dynamics.

claim: Dendritic spines constitute computational units of information processing that underlie essentially all higher brain functions.
source: They constitute computational units of information processing that underlie essentially all higher brain functions (Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Sala and Segal, 2014; Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004) and play a crucial role in brain disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Alzheimer's disease (Dorostkar et al., 2015; Südhof, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Dendritic spines play a crucial role in brain disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Alzheimer's disease.
source: They constitute computational units of information processing that underlie essentially all higher brain functions (Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Sala and Segal, 2014; Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004) and play a crucial role in brain disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and Alzheimer's disease (Dorostkar et al., 2015; Südhof, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on spine dysfunction in disease.

claim: The size of spine heads scales with synaptic strength.
source: Spine structure is closely linked to synapse function, as the size of spine heads scales with synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Noguchi et al., 2011) and the shape and number of spines can be modified by the induction of synaptic plasticity (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Nägerl et al., 2004; Tønnesen et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2004) and by sensory experience (Holtmaat et al., 2006; Keck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The shape and number of spines can be modified by the induction of synaptic plasticity.
source: Spine structure is closely linked to synapse function, as the size of spine heads scales with synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Noguchi et al., 2011) and the shape and number of spines can be modified by the induction of synaptic plasticity (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Nägerl et al., 2004; Tønnesen et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2004) and by sensory experience (Holtmaat et al., 2006; Keck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to plasticity studies.

claim: The shape and number of spines can be modified by sensory experience.
source: Spine structure is closely linked to synapse function, as the size of spine heads scales with synaptic strength (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Noguchi et al., 2011) and the shape and number of spines can be modified by the induction of synaptic plasticity (Matsuzaki et al., 2001; Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Nägerl et al., 2004; Tønnesen et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2004) and by sensory experience (Holtmaat et al., 2006; Keck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experience-dependent plasticity studies.

claim: Rewiring of neural circuits by spine plasticity is considered a key neurobiological mechanism of memory formation.
source: Rewiring of neural circuits by spine plasticity is considered a key neurobiological mechanism of memory formation (reviewed in [Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Sala and Segal, 2014; Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004; Kasai et al., 2010]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on the topic.

claim: Optically induced shrinkage of potentiated spines disrupts newly acquired motor skills.
source: Notably, a recent study showed that optically induced shrinkage of potentiated spines disrupts newly acquired motor skills (Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015), indicating a causal link between spine plasticity and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific experimental study.

claim: There is a causal link between spine plasticity and memory.
source: Notably, a recent study showed that optically induced shrinkage of potentiated spines disrupts newly acquired motor skills (Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015), indicating a causal link between spine plasticity and memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental study.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity of dendritic spines has been a consistent finding across mouse cortex in vivo.
source: While experience-dependent plasticity of dendritic spines has been a consistent finding across mouse cortex in vivo (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009), very little is known about it in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review of cortical spine plasticity studies.

claim: The hippocampus constitutes the archetypical memory center of the brain.
source: However, this is a major knowledge gap, because this neural structure constitutes the archetypical memory center of the brain, and hippocampal brain slices and primary cell cultures are the dominant model systems for the study of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is established neuroscience knowledge about the hippocampus.

claim: Hippocampal brain slices and primary cell cultures are the dominant model systems for the study of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
source: However, this is a major knowledge gap, because this neural structure constitutes the archetypical memory center of the brain, and hippocampal brain slices and primary cell cultures are the dominant model systems for the study of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about common experimental practices in neuroscience.

claim: Imaging dendritic spines in the hippocampus in vivo is challenging because of its remote location more than 1 mm below the surface of the mouse brain.
source: Imaging dendritic spines in the hippocampus in vivo is challenging because of its remote location more than 1 mm below the surface of the mouse brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomical location and technical challenges it poses.

claim: A pioneering study accomplished imaging of hippocampal spines with two-photon microscopy, but only over a period of a few hours.
source: A pioneering study accomplished this with two-photon (2P) microscopy, but only over a period of a few hours (Mizrahi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Approaches based on a 'hippocampal window' or micro-endoscopy enabled 'chronic' 2P imaging over several weeks.
source: Recently, approaches based on a 'hippocampal window' (Gu et al., 2014) or micro-endoscopy (Attardo et al., 2015) enabled 'chronic' 2P imaging over several weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific methodological studies.

claim: 2P microscopy inevitably lacks the spatial resolution to visualize important details of spine morphology, such as spine necks.
source: However, 2P microscopy inevitably lacks the spatial resolution to visualize important details of spine morphology, such as spine necks (Bethge et al., 2013), and even struggles to resolve individual dendritic spines on CA1 pyramidal neurons, leaving a high fraction of them undetected (Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating resolution limitations.

claim: 2P microscopy struggles to resolve individual dendritic spines on CA1 pyramidal neurons, leaving a high fraction of them undetected.
source: However, 2P microscopy inevitably lacks the spatial resolution to visualize important details of spine morphology, such as spine necks (Bethge et al., 2013), and even struggles to resolve individual dendritic spines on CA1 pyramidal neurons, leaving a high fraction of them undetected (Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Regular light microscopy typically detects a spine density of around 1 spine/µm.
source: While regular light microscopy typically detects a spine density of around 1 spine/µm (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015; Brigman et al., 2010), electron microscopy (EM) reports ~3 spines/µm on CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons in rats (Harris et al., 1992) and in stratum radiatum of mice (Bloss et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple light microscopy studies.

claim: Electron microscopy reports ~3 spines/µm on CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons in rats.
source: While regular light microscopy typically detects a spine density of around 1 spine/µm (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015; Brigman et al., 2010), electron microscopy (EM) reports ~3 spines/µm on CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons in rats (Harris et al., 1992) and in stratum radiatum of mice (Bloss et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an EM study.

claim: Electron microscopy reports ~3 spines/µm in stratum radiatum of mice.
source: While regular light microscopy typically detects a spine density of around 1 spine/µm (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015; Brigman et al., 2010), electron microscopy (EM) reports ~3 spines/µm on CA1 hippocampal pyramidal neurons in rats (Harris et al., 1992) and in stratum radiatum of mice (Bloss et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an EM study.

claim: Spine density is about ten times lower in many cortical areas compared to hippocampus, for example ~0.24 spines/µm for pyramidal neurons in layer 5 of mouse barrel cortex.
source: By comparison, spine density is about ten times lower in many cortical areas, for example ~0.24 spines/µm for pyramidal neurons in layer 5 of mouse barrel cortex (Holtmaat et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cortical spine density study.

claim: The authors used a home-built STED microscope based on 2P excitation.
source: We used a home-built STED microscope based on 2P excitation (2P-STED) (Bethge et al., 2013; Ter Veer et al., 2017) and equipped it with a long working distance objective to reach the deeply located hippocampus.
evidence: This is a methodological description with citations to previous work on the microscope design.

claim: The authors adopted a 'hippocampal window' technique where a portion of the overlying somatosensory cortex is surgically removed and replaced by a metal cylinder sealed with a cover slip.
source: We adopted a 'hippocampal window' technique (Gu et al., 2014; Schmid et al., 2016; Dombeck et al., 2010), where a portion of the overlying somatosensory cortex is surgically removed and replaced by a metal cylinder sealed with a cover slip, providing stable optical access to the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a methodological description with citations to previous work on the technique.

claim: The hippocampal window provides stable optical access to the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
source: We adopted a 'hippocampal window' technique (Gu et al., 2014; Schmid et al., 2016; Dombeck et al., 2010), where a portion of the overlying somatosensory cortex is surgically removed and replaced by a metal cylinder sealed with a cover slip, providing stable optical access to the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a claim about the functional outcome of the surgical technique.

claim: The new approach offers substantially improved spatial resolution and image quality compared to regular 2P microscopy in mouse hippocampus in vivo.
source: We demonstrate that our new approach offers substantially improved spatial resolution and image quality compared to regular 2P microscopy in mouse hippocampus in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim supported by comparative imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors used transgenic mice with fluorescently labeled pyramidal neurons.
source: Using transgenic mice with fluorescently labeled pyramidal neurons, we measured spine density on basal dendrites of pyramidal neurons in stratum oriens of the CA1 area and compared results obtained with 2P and 2P-STED microscopy in vivo as well as with STED microscopy in fixed hippocampal sections.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental model.

claim: The authors measured spine density on basal dendrites of pyramidal neurons in stratum oriens of the CA1 area.
source: Using transgenic mice with fluorescently labeled pyramidal neurons, we measured spine density on basal dendrites of pyramidal neurons in stratum oriens of the CA1 area and compared results obtained with 2P and 2P-STED microscopy in vivo as well as with STED microscopy in fixed hippocampal sections.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental measurements performed.

claim: The authors compared results obtained with 2P and 2P-STED microscopy in vivo as well as with STED microscopy in fixed hippocampal sections.
source: Using transgenic mice with fluorescently labeled pyramidal neurons, we measured spine density on basal dendrites of pyramidal neurons in stratum oriens of the CA1 area and compared results obtained with 2P and 2P-STED microscopy in vivo as well as with STED microscopy in fixed hippocampal sections.
evidence: This is a description of the comparative analysis performed.

claim: The authors carried out repetitive 2P-STED in vivo imaging over a 4-day period to measure spine turnover.
source: Furthermore, we carried out repetitive 2P-STED in vivo imaging over a 4-day period to measure spine turnover.
evidence: This is a description of the longitudinal imaging experiments.

claim: The analysis showed a two times higher spine density than reported by conventional 2P microscopy.
source: Our analysis showed a two times higher spine density than reported by conventional 2P microscopy, and around 40% of all spines turned over within 4 days, suggesting a high level of circuit remodeling in the hippocampus in vivo.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Around 40% of all spines turned over within 4 days, suggesting a high level of circuit remodeling in the hippocampus in vivo.
source: Our analysis showed a two times higher spine density than reported by conventional 2P microscopy, and around 40% of all spines turned over within 4 days, suggesting a high level of circuit remodeling in the hippocampus in vivo.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with an interpretation about circuit remodeling.

claim: Detailed morphological analysis revealed that primarily small spines were affected by spine turnover.
source: Furthermore, detailed morphological analysis revealed that primarily small spines were affected by spine turnover.
evidence: This is a finding from the morphological analysis of spine dynamics.

claim: The FWHM was 54 ± 2 nm in the x-y plane in 2P-STED mode.
source: The full-width at half maximum (FWHM) was 54 ± 2 nm in the x-y plane in 2P-STED mode, compared with 325 ± 5 nm in regular 2P mode (p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 17 beads; Figure 1C), demonstrating that our super-resolution approach delivered a six-fold nominal gain in lateral spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PSF characterization experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The FWHM was 325 ± 5 nm in regular 2P mode.
source: The full-width at half maximum (FWHM) was 54 ± 2 nm in the x-y plane in 2P-STED mode, compared with 325 ± 5 nm in regular 2P mode (p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 17 beads; Figure 1C), demonstrating that our super-resolution approach delivered a six-fold nominal gain in lateral spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from PSF characterization experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The super-resolution approach delivered a six-fold nominal gain in lateral spatial resolution.
source: The full-width at half maximum (FWHM) was 54 ± 2 nm in the x-y plane in 2P-STED mode, compared with 325 ± 5 nm in regular 2P mode (p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 17 beads; Figure 1C), demonstrating that our super-resolution approach delivered a six-fold nominal gain in lateral spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the ratio of FWHM measurements.

claim: The axial resolution remained unchanged in 2P-STED.
source: In contrast, the axial resolution remained unchanged in 2P-STED (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from axial PSF measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The authors used transgenic mice (Thy1-HYFP/+ and Thy1-MGFP/+, 4–12 months old) that expressed either GFP or YFP in a subset of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: We used transgenic mice (Thy1-HYFP/+ and Thy1-MGFP/+, 4–12 months old) that expressed either GFP or YFP in a subset of CA1 pyramidal neurons (Feng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental model with a citation to the mouse line.

claim: Spines were much more clearly delineated in 2P-STED than in 2P mode when focusing on dendrites close to the coverslip (5–20 µm).
source: Focusing on dendrites close to the coverslip (5–20 µm), spines were much more clearly delineated in 2P-STED than in 2P mode (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation supported by images in the figures.

claim: Spine necks were better resolved with 2P-STED as evidenced by paired measurements of spine neck widths (2P-STED: 147 ± 8 nm; 2P: 369 ± 6 nm; p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 35 spine necks, 17 dendrites, 6 mice).
source: In particular, spine necks were better resolved with 2P-STED as evidenced by paired measurements of spine neck widths (2P-STED: 147 ± 8 nm; 2P: 369 ± 6 nm; p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 35 spine necks, 17 dendrites, 6 mice; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement comparing spine neck widths between imaging modes.

claim: Image distortions caused by animal breathing and heartbeat normally pose a serious challenge for imaging in vivo, in particular STED microscopy.
source: Image distortions caused by animal breathing and heartbeat normally pose a serious challenge for imaging in vivo, in particular STED microscopy, which is especially sensitive to brain motion due to its high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about known technical challenges in in vivo imaging.

claim: STED microscopy is especially sensitive to brain motion due to its high spatial resolution.
source: Image distortions caused by animal breathing and heartbeat normally pose a serious challenge for imaging in vivo, in particular STED microscopy, which is especially sensitive to brain motion due to its high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between spatial resolution and motion sensitivity.

claim: The authors only encountered mild levels of image blur, making it not necessary to apply motion correction.
source: However, we only encountered mild levels of image blur (Figure 1—video 1), making it not necessary to apply motion correction (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments supported by video data.

claim: There was a significant difference in spine density between 2P-STED and 2P mode (2P-STED: 2.13 ± 0.10 µm−1; 2P: 1.61 ± 0.07 µm−1; p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 82 dendrites, 6 mice).
source: There was a significant difference between the two modes (2P-STED: 2.13 ± 0.10 µm−1; 2P: 1.61 ± 0.07 µm−1; p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 82 dendrites, 6 mice; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), where 2P-STED detected on average 32% more spines than 2P in a direct comparison (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of spine density measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: 2P-STED detected on average 32% more spines than 2P in a direct comparison.
source: There was a significant difference between the two modes (2P-STED: 2.13 ± 0.10 µm−1; 2P: 1.61 ± 0.07 µm−1; p<0.0001, paired t-test; n = 82 dendrites, 6 mice; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), where 2P-STED detected on average 32% more spines than 2P in a direct comparison (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the spine density measurements.

claim: The increase in detected spines was due to the improved detection or discrimination of (1) spines that either had short necks or that extended into the z-direction, which were otherwise obscured by the fluorescence signal of the dendritic shaft, and (2) closely clustered spines, which appeared merged in the 2P images.
source: This increase was due to the improved detection or discrimination of (1) spines that either had short necks or that extended into the z-direction, which were otherwise obscured by the fluorescence signal of the dendritic shaft, and (2) closely clustered spines, which appeared merged in the 2P images (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on visual inspection of the images.

claim: The 2P-based mean value for spine density (1.61 µm−1) is around 45% higher than the values reported in the light microscopy literature (~1.1 µm−1).
source: While our 2P-based mean value for spine density (1.61 µm−1) is around 45% higher than the values reported in the light microscopy literature (~1.1 µm−1) (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015), the mean value based on 2P-STED is about twice as large as this (2.13 µm−1).
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' measurements to literature values.

claim: The mean value based on 2P-STED is about twice as large as the values reported in the light microscopy literature (~1.1 µm−1).
source: While our 2P-based mean value for spine density (1.61 µm−1) is around 45% higher than the values reported in the light microscopy literature (~1.1 µm−1) (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015), the mean value based on 2P-STED is about twice as large as this (2.13 µm−1).
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' measurements to literature values.

claim: Using a commercial STED microscope with one-photon excitation, the authors measured a spine density of 2.68 ± 0.08 µm−1 in fixed brain slices (n = 37 dendrites, 6 mice).
source: Using a commercial STED microscope with one-photon excitation, we measured a density of 2.68 ± 0.08 µm−1 (n = 37 dendrites, 6 mice; Figure 2D), which comes closer to the values reported by EM.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from fixed tissue imaging.

claim: The spine density measured in fixed tissue comes closer to the values reported by EM.
source: Using a commercial STED microscope with one-photon excitation, we measured a density of 2.68 ± 0.08 µm−1 (n = 37 dendrites, 6 mice; Figure 2D), which comes closer to the values reported by EM.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' measurements to EM literature values.

claim: According to a geometrical model accounting for limited axial resolution, about a quarter of the spines could not be detected in vivo.
source: According to the model, which took into account the actual dimensions of dendritic morphology and the PSF of the microscope, about a quarter of the spines could not be detected in vivo because of this problem.
evidence: This is a result from a theoretical model based on geometric considerations.

claim: Correcting the measured values by the fraction of undetectable spines, the authors calculated a spine density of 2.91 ± 0.14 µm−1 for the in vivo data and 3.15 ± 0.09 µm−1 for the fixed tissue data.
source: Correcting the measured values by this fraction, we calculated a spine density of 2.91 ± 0.14 µm−1 for the in vivo data and 3.15 ± 0.09 µm−1 for the fixed tissue data (Figure 2F), which effectively closed the gap to the 'ground truth' EM values.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the model correction applied to the measured data.

claim: The corrected spine density values effectively closed the gap to the 'ground truth' EM values.
source: Correcting the measured values by this fraction, we calculated a spine density of 2.91 ± 0.14 µm−1 for the in vivo data and 3.15 ± 0.09 µm−1 for the fixed tissue data (Figure 2F), which effectively closed the gap to the 'ground truth' EM values.
evidence: This is a comparison of corrected values to EM literature values.

claim: The authors performed repeated 2P-STED imaging of individual dendritic stretches over 4 days (day 0, 2 and 4).
source: To determine the kinetics of spine emergence and elimination, which is a matter of controversy (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015), we performed repeated 2P-STED imaging of individual dendritic stretches over 4 days (day 0, 2 and 4; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the longitudinal imaging protocol.

claim: The kinetics of spine emergence and elimination is a matter of controversy.
source: To determine the kinetics of spine emergence and elimination, which is a matter of controversy (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015), we performed repeated 2P-STED imaging of individual dendritic stretches over 4 days (day 0, 2 and 4; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statement about conflicting findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The authors used tissue landmarks such as blood vessels, fluorescent cell bodies and dendrites to retrieve a particular dendrite in consecutive imaging sessions.
source: To retrieve a particular dendrite in consecutive imaging sessions, we used tissue landmarks such as blood vessels, fluorescent cell bodies and dendrites.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach for longitudinal tracking.

claim: The average spine density remained stable over the entire observation period (day 0: 2.31 ± 0.10 µm−1; day 2: 2.28 ± 0.08 µm−1; day 4: 2.30 ± 0.10 µm−1; n = 14 dendrites, 3 mice).
source: First, we quantified the average spine density for each time point, which remained stable over the entire observation period (day 0: 2.31 ± 0.10 µm−1; day 2: 2.28 ± 0.08 µm−1; day 4: 2.30 ± 0.10 µm−1; n = 14 dendrites, 3 mice; Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: The survival fraction was 78.1 ± 3.6% for day 2, and 60.8 ± 3.4% for day 4.
source: The survival fraction was 78.1 ± 3.6% for day 2, and 60.8 ± 3.4% for day 4 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of spine persistence over time.

claim: The fraction of lost spines was 21.2 ± 3.6% from day 0 to 2, and 24.7 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4.
source: The fraction of lost spines was 21.2 ± 3.6% from day 0 to 2, and 24.7 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4 (Figure 3D), while the fraction of new spines from day 0 to 2 was 20.4 ± 2.6%, and 21.9 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of spine loss over time.

claim: The fraction of new spines from day 0 to 2 was 20.4 ± 2.6%, and 21.9 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4.
source: The fraction of lost spines was 21.2 ± 3.6% from day 0 to 2, and 24.7 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4 (Figure 3D), while the fraction of new spines from day 0 to 2 was 20.4 ± 2.6%, and 21.9 ± 3.0% from day 2 to 4 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of spine formation over time.

claim: The rates of spine loss and gain were balanced and did not change over the sessions, which is consistent with the constant spine density observed.
source: These results indicate that the rates of spine loss and gain were balanced and did not change over the sessions, which is consistent with the constant spine density we observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the turnover data in relation to the stable density measurements.

claim: Spine turnover was less visible in 2P mode, amounting to a survival fraction of 74.9 ± 2.2% after 4 days.
source: By comparison, spine turnover was less visible in 2P mode, amounting to a survival fraction of 74.9 ± 2.2% after 4 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of turnover measurements between imaging modes.

claim: In cortex, spines with a large head have been shown to be more stable than filopodial and thin spines.
source: In cortex, spines with a large head have been shown to be more stable than filopodial and thin spines (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Knott et al., 2006), but it is unknown whether such a link also exists for the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cortical spine stability studies.

claim: It is unknown whether a link between spine size and stability exists for the hippocampus.
source: In cortex, spines with a large head have been shown to be more stable than filopodial and thin spines (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Knott et al., 2006), but it is unknown whether such a link also exists for the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a statement about a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Spines that were visible on all three imaging sessions (Persistence >2 days) had larger heads than spines that were visible on only one or two sessions (Persistence ≤2 days).
source: Spines that were visible on all three imaging sessions (Persistence >2 days) had larger heads than spines that were visible on only one or two sessions (Persistence ≤2 days), suggesting that small spines are more short-lived than large ones (>2 days: 0.03 μm3 and 0.01–0.06 μm3 versus ≤ 2 days: 0.02 μm3 and 0.01–0.04 μm3, median and interquartile range; Figure 4A,B; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of spine head volumes based on persistence.

claim: Small spines are more short-lived than large ones.
source: Spines that were visible on all three imaging sessions (Persistence >2 days) had larger heads than spines that were visible on only one or two sessions (Persistence ≤2 days), suggesting that small spines are more short-lived than large ones (>2 days: 0.03 μm3 and 0.01–0.06 μm3 versus ≤ 2 days: 0.02 μm3 and 0.01–0.04 μm3, median and interquartile range; Figure 4A,B; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the relationship between spine size and persistence.

claim: A cluster analysis revealed at least three distinct populations of spines.
source: A cluster analysis ('Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering' analysis based on Euclidian distance in the parameter space, see Materials and methods) revealed at least three distinct populations of spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which resemble the different categories commonly used in the literature to classify dendritic spines ('small' ≅ cluster 1, 'thin' ≅ cluster 2 and 'mushroom-like' ≅ cluster 3; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from statistical cluster analysis of morphological parameters.

claim: The three spine clusters resemble the different categories commonly used in the literature to classify dendritic spines ('small' ≅ cluster 1, 'thin' ≅ cluster 2 and 'mushroom-like' ≅ cluster 3).
source: A cluster analysis ('Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering' analysis based on Euclidian distance in the parameter space, see Materials and methods) revealed at least three distinct populations of spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which resemble the different categories commonly used in the literature to classify dendritic spines ('small' ≅ cluster 1, 'thin' ≅ cluster 2 and 'mushroom-like' ≅ cluster 3; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation relating the cluster analysis results to established spine classifications.

claim: Around 50% of more persistent spines exhibited a mushroom-like morphology.
source: Notably, whereas around 50% of more persistent spines exhibited a mushroom-like morphology, less persistent spines rarely (7%) belonged to this category (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cluster analysis related to spine persistence.

claim: Less persistent spines rarely (7%) belonged to the mushroom-like category.
source: Notably, whereas around 50% of more persistent spines exhibited a mushroom-like morphology, less persistent spines rarely (7%) belonged to this category (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cluster analysis related to spine persistence.

claim: Within cluster 3, less persistent spines had on average smaller heads and lower head to neck diameter ratios.
source: Even within cluster 3, less persistent spines had on average smaller heads and lower head to neck diameter ratios (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of morphological parameters within a spine cluster.

claim: The authors established chronic super-resolution imaging of dendritic spines in the intact hippocampus of living mice.
source: We established chronic super-resolution imaging of dendritic spines in the intact hippocampus of living mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the methodological achievement.

claim: STED microscopy has been used before for imaging dendritic spines in vivo, but only in superficial cortical layers and for one-off and acute imaging sessions.
source: STED microscopy has been used before for imaging dendritic spines in vivo, but only in superficial cortical layers and for one-off and acute imaging sessions (Berning et al., 2012; Willig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous STED imaging studies.

claim: Dendritic spines commonly serve as a morphological proxy for excitatory synapses.
source: Dendritic spines commonly serve as a morphological proxy for excitatory synapses, allowing inferences on synaptic strength and functional connectivity, for instance when their shape, size or number change over the course of an electrophysiological or behavioral experiment (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004; Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience supported by citations.

claim: Spines have nanoscale dimensions and are densely packed in light scattering tissue, making accurate and quantitative anatomical readout difficult to obtain.
source: However, since spines have nanoscale dimensions and are densely packed in light scattering tissue, an accurate and quantitative anatomical readout is oftentimes difficult to obtain (Bethge et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges in spine imaging, supported by a citation.

claim: Spine density has been shown to vary between 2 and 4 µm−1 on proximal apical dendrites in stratum radiatum in adult rats according to serial section transmission EM.
source: Spine density has been shown to vary between 2 and 4 µm−1 on proximal apical dendrites in stratum radiatum in adult rats (Harris et al., 1992; Harris and Stevens, 1989) and mice (Bloss et al., 2018) according to serial section transmission EM, and between 2 and 3 µm−1 on basal oblique dendrites in stratum oriens in adult mice according to array tomography (Bloss et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to EM studies.

claim: Spine density has been shown to vary between 2 and 4 µm−1 on proximal apical dendrites in stratum radiatum in adult mice according to serial section transmission EM.
source: Spine density has been shown to vary between 2 and 4 µm−1 on proximal apical dendrites in stratum radiatum in adult rats (Harris et al., 1992; Harris and Stevens, 1989) and mice (Bloss et al., 2018) according to serial section transmission EM, and between 2 and 3 µm−1 on basal oblique dendrites in stratum oriens in adult mice according to array tomography (Bloss et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an EM study.

claim: Spine density varies between 2 and 3 µm−1 on basal oblique dendrites in stratum oriens in adult mice according to array tomography.
source: Spine density has been shown to vary between 2 and 4 µm−1 on proximal apical dendrites in stratum radiatum in adult rats (Harris et al., 1992; Harris and Stevens, 1989) and mice (Bloss et al., 2018) according to serial section transmission EM, and between 2 and 3 µm−1 on basal oblique dendrites in stratum oriens in adult mice according to array tomography (Bloss et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an array tomography study.

claim: The spine densities detected in stratum oriens lie within the range of EM and array tomography measurements.
source: By comparison, the spine densities we detected in stratum oriens lie within the range of these measurements, while the two recent in vivo 2P microscopy studies reported values less than half the amount (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' measurements to literature values.

claim: Two recent in vivo 2P microscopy studies reported spine density values less than half the amount of EM measurements.
source: By comparison, the spine densities we detected in stratum oriens lie within the range of these measurements, while the two recent in vivo 2P microscopy studies reported values less than half the amount (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of literature values from different imaging modalities.

claim: The STED approach only improved the lateral resolution, so spines that protruded into the axial direction were still difficult to detect.
source: As our STED approach only improved the lateral resolution, spines that protruded into the axial direction were still difficult to detect, explaining why our density values are still below those reported by EM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the technical limitations and their impact on measurements.

claim: Correcting the data based on a simple geometric model removed the residual difference between STED and EM measurements.
source: Indeed, correcting our data based on a simple geometric model removed the residual difference.
evidence: This is a result from applying the geometric correction model to the data.

claim: Ongoing technical advances in 3D beam shaping will improve axial resolution and should enable nearly complete spine detection in vivo.
source: In the near future, our method stands to benefit from ongoing technical advances, for instance in 3D beam shaping, which will improve axial resolution (Gould et al., 2012; Patton et al., 2016), and should enable nearly complete spine detection in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation about future technical improvements supported by citations.

claim: The authors could only image spines in the stratum oriens within 20 µm from the cover slip; beyond this distance, image quality degraded rapidly.
source: We could only image spines in the stratum oriens within 20 µm from the cover slip; beyond this distance, image quality degraded rapidly.
evidence: This is an observation about the depth limitation of the imaging approach.

claim: The depth limitation was likely due to optical aberrations caused by mismatches in refractive index between the immersion medium, the glass cover slip and the sample.
source: This depth limitation was likely due to optical aberrations caused by mismatches in refractive index between the immersion medium, the glass cover slip and the sample (n ≈ 1.37 for brain tissue [Lue et al., 2007]).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the depth limitation, supported by a citation about tissue refractive index.

claim: The new objective did not have a correction collar to reduce spherical aberrations, which otherwise probably would have permitted greater imaging depth.
source: Unlike other objectives we have used for STED microscopy in brain tissue (Bethge et al., 2013; Urban et al., 2011), the new objective did not have a correction collar to reduce spherical aberrations, which otherwise probably would have permitted greater imaging depth.
evidence: This is a speculation about how a different objective design might have improved performance.

claim: The use of adaptive optics is bound to allow for deeper imaging and thus to reach dendrites in stratum radiatum and other areas of the hippocampus.
source: However, the use of adaptive optics is bound to allow for deeper imaging (Ji, 2017) and thus to reach dendrites in stratum radiatum and other areas of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a speculation about future technical improvements supported by a citation.

claim: The near total absence of motion artifacts in the images was primarily due to two effects: the implanted metal tube probably stabilized the brain mechanically, and blood pulsations are likely much weaker in the hippocampus where the vasculature is mostly formed by capillaries.
source: We suspect that the near total absence of motion artifacts in the images was primarily due to two effects: firstly, the implanted metal tube probably stabilized the brain mechanically, and secondly, blood pulsations are likely much weaker in the hippocampus where the vasculature is mostly formed by capillaries and has fewer large arteries than in superficial cortex (Marinković et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for reduced motion artifacts, with one part supported by a citation.

claim: Faithful and complete detection of spines across space and time is absolutely critical for an accurate assessment of spine turnover.
source: Faithful and complete detection of spines across space and time is absolutely critical for an accurate assessment of spine turnover.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the requirements for accurate turnover measurements.

claim: Failure to distinguish closely spaced spines will lead to an underestimate of spine turnover.
source: Failure to distinguish closely spaced spines will lead to an underestimate of spine turnover, because events of individual spines appearing or disappearing within a merged cluster will inevitably be missed, giving a false impression of spine stability (Attardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a logical inference about how resolution limitations affect turnover measurements, supported by a citation.

claim: Temporal fluctuations, for instance when spines rotate in or out of the optical axis, will lead to an overestimate of spine turnover.
source: Conversely, temporal fluctuations, for instance when spines rotate in or out of the optical axis, will lead to an overestimate of spine turnover.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how certain artifacts can affect turnover measurements.

claim: Biased detection of large spines might distort the measurements of spine turnover as large spines are reportedly less structurally plastic than small spines.
source: Moreover, biased detection of large spines might distort the measurements of spine turnover as large spines are reportedly less structurally plastic than small spines (Matsuzaki et al., 2004), as we have also shown here.
evidence: This is an inference about how detection bias affects turnover measurements, supported by a citation and the authors' own data.

claim: Two recent studies that pioneered chronic imaging in the hippocampus in vivo reported very different lifetimes for spines on apical and basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: The spine detection problem was highlighted by two recent studies that pioneered chronic imaging in the hippocampus in vivo (Gu et al., 2014; Attardo et al., 2015) and reported very different lifetimes for spines on apical and basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about conflicting findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The study by Gu et al. reported that ~96% of spines survived for at least 16 days in stratum radiatum.
source: The study by Gu et al. (Gu et al., 2014) reported that ~96% of spines survived for at least 16 days in stratum radiatum, whereas the study by Attardo et al. (Attardo et al., 2015) predicted that the entire population of spines in stratum oriens turned over within a month.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The study by Attardo et al. predicted that the entire population of spines in stratum oriens turned over within a month.
source: The study by Gu et al. (Gu et al., 2014) reported that ~96% of spines survived for at least 16 days in stratum radiatum, whereas the study by Attardo et al. (Attardo et al., 2015) predicted that the entire population of spines in stratum oriens turned over within a month.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Both studies used 2P microscopy with relatively low NA optics and presented images of comparable quality, reporting similar average spine densities (~1.1 µm−1) that were stable over time.
source: Both studies used 2P microscopy with relatively low NA optics and presented images of comparable quality, reporting similar average spine densities (~1.1 µm−1) that were stable over time.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological approaches in the cited studies.

claim: Gu et al. assessed spine turnover directly from the 2P images.
source: While Gu et al. assessed spine turnover directly from the 2P images, Attardo et al. went a step further and used mathematical modeling to account for the effect of merged spines on apparent spine turnover.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach used in a cited study.

claim: Attardo et al. used mathematical modeling to account for the effect of merged spines on apparent spine turnover.
source: While Gu et al. assessed spine turnover directly from the 2P images, Attardo et al. went a step further and used mathematical modeling to account for the effect of merged spines on apparent spine turnover.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach used in a cited study.

claim: Without applying the mathematical correction, the survival fraction in the Attardo et al. study was around 80% after 21 days.
source: Importantly though, without applying the mathematical correction, their survival fraction was around 80% after 21 days, indicating that direct analysis of 2P images is highly problematic when it comes to establishing spine turnover rates.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Direct analysis of 2P images is highly problematic when it comes to establishing spine turnover rates.
source: Importantly though, without applying the mathematical correction, their survival fraction was around 80% after 21 days, indicating that direct analysis of 2P images is highly problematic when it comes to establishing spine turnover rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of corrected and uncorrected turnover measurements.

claim: The super-resolution approach documented a spine survival fraction of 60% after 4 days, providing direct and unambiguous evidence that spines can turn over extremely rapidly in CA1 stratum oriens.
source: Our super-resolution approach documented a spine survival fraction of 60% after 4 days, providing direct and unambiguous evidence that spines can turn over extremely rapidly in CA1 stratum oriens, supporting one of the main modeling-based conclusions of the Attardo et al. study.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings and their interpretation.

claim: The findings support one of the main modeling-based conclusions of the Attardo et al. study.
source: Our super-resolution approach documented a spine survival fraction of 60% after 4 days, providing direct and unambiguous evidence that spines can turn over extremely rapidly in CA1 stratum oriens, supporting one of the main modeling-based conclusions of the Attardo et al. study.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' findings to a cited study.

claim: It is hard to extrapolate the results in time and determine the extent to which the observed kinetics hold for the entire spine population since only three time points over a relatively short period were imaged.
source: However, since we imaged just three time points over a relatively short period, it is hard to extrapolate our results in time and determine the extent to which the observed kinetics hold for the entire spine population.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the experimental design.

claim: The observation that larger spines were more stable is a sign for the existence of multiple, kinetically distinct spine populations.
source: In fact, our observation that larger spines were more stable is a sign for the existence of multiple, kinetically distinct spine populations, unlike the Attardo et al. study, which argued for a single population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morphology-turnover relationship data.

claim: The Attardo et al. study argued for a single spine population.
source: In fact, our observation that larger spines were more stable is a sign for the existence of multiple, kinetically distinct spine populations, unlike the Attardo et al. study, which argued for a single population.
evidence: This is a summary of a conclusion from a cited study.

claim: The authors did not observe any overt signs of phototoxicity, such as dendritic 'blebbing' during short time-lapse sequences and across the imaging sessions.
source: We did not observe any overt signs of phototoxicity, such as dendritic 'blebbing' during short time-lapse sequences and across the imaging sessions (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: The absence of phototoxicity together with the fact that spine density remained constant indicates that the observed kinetics were real and not an artifact induced by the hippocampal window approach or 2P-STED imaging.
source: This absence together with the fact that spine density remained constant indicates that the observed kinetics were real and not an artifact induced by our hippocampal window approach or 2P-STED imaging.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple observations to validate the findings.

claim: The use of the NMDA-receptor antagonist ketamine could be problematic given the important role of NMDA-receptors in hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
source: The use of the NMDA-receptor antagonist ketamine could be problematic given the important role of NMDA-receptors in hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential confound based on known pharmacology.

claim: It is unlikely that the results were compromised by ketamine as the drug was applied only for a couple of hours per imaging session and no plasticity was induced.
source: However, as the drug was applied only for a couple of hours per imaging session and we did not induce any plasticity, it is unlikely that our results were compromised by it.
evidence: This is an inference about the minimal impact of the anesthetic based on the experimental conditions.

claim: The use of more innocuous drugs or performing the experiments with non-anesthetized and head-fixed animals will be preferable in the future.
source: The use of more innocuous drugs or performing the experiments with non-anesthetized and head-fixed animals will be preferable in the future.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental improvements.

claim: The authors did not image in the stratum radiatum, so they do not know to what extent the divergence in spine turnover between stratum radiatum and stratum oriens reflects methodological or genuine anatomical or physiological differences.
source: As we did not image in the stratum radiatum, we do not know to what extent the divergence in spine turnover between stratum radiatum reported by Gu et al. and stratum oriens (Attardo et al. and our data) reflects methodological or genuine anatomical or physiological differences.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations in interpreting differences between studies.

claim: Stratum radiatum primarily receives input from CA3.
source: In fact, stratum radiatum primarily receives input from CA3 (Somogyi, 2010; Cappaert et al., 2014), whereas stratum oriens also has afferents from entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stratum oriens has afferents from entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
source: In fact, stratum radiatum primarily receives input from CA3 (Somogyi, 2010; Cappaert et al., 2014), whereas stratum oriens also has afferents from entorhinal cortex and amygdala.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: There may be intrinsic differences in the postsynaptic neuron which account for dendrite-specific spine turnover.
source: In addition, there may be intrinsic differences in the postsynaptic neuron, which account for dendrite-specific spine turnover.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms underlying regional differences.

claim: The finding that hippocampal dendrites are subject to ongoing intense anatomical remodeling supports the view of the hippocampus as a highly dynamic structure designed to encode and process new memories, but not as a long-term repository of information.
source: Our finding that hippocampal dendrites are subject to ongoing intense anatomical remodeling supports the view of the hippocampus as a highly dynamic structure designed to encode and process new memories, but not as a long-term repository of information (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of hippocampal function, supported by a citation.

claim: The situation may be quite different in cortical areas, where typically a large fraction of spines is stable for many weeks in adult mice.
source: The situation may be quite different in cortical areas, where typically a large fraction of spines is stable for many weeks in adult mice (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Majewska et al., 2006; Trachtenberg et al., 2002), unless they are subjected to behavioral training (Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009) or sensory manipulations (Hofer et al., 2009; Keck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to cortical spine stability based on cited literature.

claim: Cortical spines can become unstable when subjected to behavioral training or sensory manipulations.
source: The situation may be quite different in cortical areas, where typically a large fraction of spines is stable for many weeks in adult mice (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Majewska et al., 2006; Trachtenberg et al., 2002), unless they are subjected to behavioral training (Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009) or sensory manipulations (Hofer et al., 2009; Keck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about experience-dependent plasticity in cortex, supported by citations.

claim: Whether and how spine turnover actually reflects memory-relevant functional adaptations in synaptic strength and connectivity remains to be determined.
source: However, whether and how spine turnover actually reflects memory-relevant functional adaptations in synaptic strength and connectivity remains to be determined.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an open question in the field.

claim: The present work adds up to a substantial advance for the study of hippocampal synapses in living mice, extending the scope of super-resolution microscopy to a deeply embedded brain structure that is critical for memory function.
source: In summary, the present work adds up to a substantial advance for the study of hippocampal synapses in living mice, extending the scope of super-resolution microscopy to a deeply embedded brain structure that is critical for memory function.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The chronic super-resolution imaging approach creates manifold opportunities to study the neurobiological mechanisms and functional significance of spine plasticity in the mammalian brain by correlating spine-level structural changes with genetic, molecular and behavioral interventions and assays.
source: By correlating spine-level structural changes with genetic, molecular and behavioral interventions and assays, our chronic super-resolution imaging approach creates manifold opportunities to study the neurobiological mechanisms and functional significance of spine plasticity in the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications and impact of the developed method.
